## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Kaṅkhākathā* ("Discourse on Doubt" or "Uncertainty") is the third debate of the second chapter (*vagga*) of the *Kathāvatthu* in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka [SuttaCentral]. It forms part of the classical refutation of the controversial "Five Points" traditionally attributed to Mahādeva, concerning the putative imperfections of the arahant [Williams 2000; Skorupski 1991]. In the sequence of debates presented in the *Kathāvatthu*, the thesis of an arahant having doubt or uncertainty (*kaṅkhā*) constitutes the third point, situated immediately after the debates on an arahant receiving impure emissions from others (*parūpahāra*, Kv 2.1) and being subject to ignorance (*aññāṇa*, Kv 2.2), and preceding the debate on guidance or induction of comprehension by others (*paravitāraṇā*, Kv 2.4) [Williams 2000; Skorupski 1991; Yao 2005]. While several non-Theravāda northern traditions, such as accounts recorded in Chinese and Tibetan treatises, place doubt before or after other items in the five-point mnemonic verse (*parūpahāro aññāṇaṁ kaṅkhā paravitāraṇā...*), the Pāli text treats *kaṅkhā* as its third successive topic, an ordering also attested in Vinītadeva's work [Williams 2000; Skorupski 1991; Yao 2005].
Textual reuse analyses show that the *Kaṅkhākathā* shares extensive formulaic refutations with adjacent debates in the *Kathāvatthu*, especially the *Paravitāraṇakathā* (Kv 2.4, sharing over 28,000 characters), the *Aññāṇakathā* (Kv 2.2, over 25,000 characters), and the *Parūpahārakathā* (Kv 2.1) [DharmaNexus]. Canonical sutta material is closely interwoven into the debate, with curated parallels and matches aligning with passages from the *Sabbāsava Sutta* (MN 2), the *Upanisa Sutta* (SN 12.23), the *Vāsijaṭasutta* (SN 22.101), the *Āsavakkhayasutta* (SN 56.25 / Iti 102), and the *Mahākhandhaka* (Kd 1), as well as cross-tradition alignments with Sanskrit versions of the *Udānavarga* (such as the Subaši manuscript) and related Chinese and Tibetan canonical texts [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
